source.title: Resolve Conflict Calmly
source.attribution: A Reborn guide drawing on Arizona State University Wellness, the Gottman Institute, Harvard's Program on Negotiation and Greater Good Science Center.
source.notes: Written by Reborn in our own words; no text copied. References: Arizona State University Wellness, Conflict resolution, https://wellness.asu.edu/explore-wellness/mind/emotional-well-being/conflict-resolution; The Gottman Institute, The Four Horsemen, https://www.gottman.com/blog/the-four-horsemen-recognizing-criticism-contempt-defensiveness-and-stonewalling/; Harvard Program on Negotiation, Conflict resolution strategies, https://www.pon.harvard.edu/daily/conflict-resolution/conflict-resolution-strategies/; Greater Good Science Center, What is forgiveness, https://greatergood.berkeley.edu/topic/forgiveness/definition

cards.title: See conflict as a problem to solve together, not a fight to win
cards.body:
Disagreements are a normal part of any close relationship, at home, at work or among friends. Two people who care about different things will sometimes clash. The goal is not to avoid conflict forever, but to handle it in a way that leaves you both closer rather than more hurt.

When you treat an argument as a contest, someone has to lose, and the loser usually carries resentment. When you treat it as a shared problem, you are on the same side, facing the issue together.

This guide walks through a calm, practical way to do that: steady yourself first, speak without blame, listen properly, find what you both want, agree on a plan, and repair the relationship afterwards.
cards.apply_it: Think of one recent disagreement. Write it as a shared problem: 'How can we both...?' instead of 'How do I get them to...?'

quiz.question: What is the healthiest way to view a conflict?
options: As a shared problem you solve together
As a contest you need to win
As something to avoid at all costs
quiz.explanation: When you face the issue together, nobody has to lose, and the relationship can come out stronger.

cards.title: Pause before you react so your calm brain can do the talking
cards.body:
When you feel attacked, your body gets ready to fight: your heart races, your face gets hot and your thinking narrows. In that state it is easy to say something you will regret, and hard to really hear the other person.

So pause first. Take a few slow breaths, count to ten, or unclench your jaw and hands. If you are too upset to think clearly, it is fine to say, 'I want to sort this out, but I need twenty minutes to calm down first.' Then do something soothing, like a short walk, and come back as promised.

A break is not running away. Saying when you will return is what makes it respectful rather than dismissive.
cards.apply_it: Choose a calm-down phrase now, such as 'Give me a few minutes and I'll come back,' so it is ready the next time you feel heated.

quiz.question: What makes taking a break during an argument respectful?
options: Leaving without a word
Waiting until the other person apologises
Saying you need time and when you will come back
Changing the subject
quiz.explanation: Naming a time to return shows you still care about solving the problem, not just escaping it.

cards.title: Choose a good time and place for a hard conversation
cards.body:
The same words can land very differently depending on when and where you say them. Raising a sore point when someone is rushing out of the door, hungry, exhausted or in front of other people almost guarantees a defensive reply.

Instead, ask for a time that suits you both: 'There's something I'd like to talk through. Is tonight after dinner good?' Pick somewhere private and quiet, where neither of you feels watched or trapped. Put phones away so you can give each other full attention.

This also gives both of you a moment to think about what you really want to say. A planned conversation tends to be calmer and shorter than one that explodes out of nowhere.
cards.apply_it: If something is bothering you, ask the person today for a calm, private time to talk about it this week.

quiz.question: Which is the best moment to raise a difficult issue?
options: At an agreed time, somewhere private and quiet
When they are tired and rushing out
In front of friends so there are witnesses
quiz.explanation: A calm, private, agreed time lowers defensiveness and helps both people listen.

cards.title: Attack the problem, not the person
cards.body:
There is a big difference between a complaint and a criticism. A complaint is about a specific action: 'The dishes were left in the sink again.' A criticism is about someone's character: 'You're so lazy and selfish.' The first can be fixed; the second makes people defend themselves.

Relationship researchers have found that personal attacks, mockery, eye-rolling and sarcasm are especially damaging, because they signal contempt. Once someone feels looked down on, they stop listening and start protecting themselves.

Keep to the specific behaviour and its effect. Avoid words like 'always' and 'never', which are rarely true and invite an argument about the exaggeration instead of the real issue.
cards.apply_it: Next time you are annoyed, check your words: are you describing a specific action, or labelling the person? Rewrite one label as an action.

quiz.question: Which of these is a complaint about a behaviour rather than an attack on a person?
options: You never think about anyone but yourself
The rent was paid late this month and I got a warning letter
You're useless with money
You always ruin everything
quiz.explanation: It names a specific event and its effect, without labelling the person's character.

cards.title: Use I-statements to say how you feel without blaming
cards.body:
An I-statement describes your experience instead of accusing the other person. A simple pattern is: I feel (emotion) when (specific action) because (the effect on you), and I would like (what you are asking for).

For example: 'I feel stressed when plans change at the last minute because I've already arranged my day. I'd like us to check with each other first.' Compare that with 'You're so inconsiderate', which is likely to start a fight.

I-statements work because nobody can argue with how you feel, and they give the other person a clear, fair request they can actually meet. Keep your tone gentle and your request specific.
cards.apply_it: Write one I-statement for something that bothers you, using: I feel... when... because... I'd like...

quiz.question: Which is a well-formed I-statement?
options: I feel you are being rude
You make me angry
I think you're wrong
I feel hurt when I'm interrupted because I lose my thought. I'd like to finish first
quiz.explanation: It names a feeling, a specific action, its effect and a clear request, without blaming.

cards.title: Listen to understand, not to plan your reply
cards.body:
Most of us half-listen in an argument while we prepare our comeback. The other person can tell, and they repeat themselves more loudly. Real listening breaks that cycle.

Give your full attention. Let them finish without interrupting. Ask open questions such as 'What part upset you most?' or 'What would help?' Try to discover what is underneath the complaint: often a dispute about chores or money is really about feeling unappreciated, unheard or not trusted.

You do not have to agree in order to understand. Understanding simply means you could explain their view in a way they would recognise. That alone often lowers the temperature a great deal.
cards.apply_it: In your next disagreement, ask one open question before you give your own view.

quiz.question: What does listening to understand mean?
options: Grasping their view well enough to explain it back
Staying silent while you plan your answer
Agreeing with everything they say
quiz.explanation: You can understand someone's view without agreeing with it, and that understanding calms things down.

cards.title: Reflect back what you heard before you respond
cards.body:
Reflecting means putting the other person's point into your own words and checking you got it right. For example: 'So you felt left out when I made the plans without asking you. Is that right?'

This simple step does three things. It proves you were listening. It catches misunderstandings early, before you argue about something they never said. And it helps the other person feel heard, which makes them far more willing to listen to you in return.

Keep it short and avoid adding your own spin, like 'So you're saying I'm a terrible friend.' If they correct you, thank them and try again. Once they agree you have it, it is your turn to share your side.
cards.apply_it: Today, reflect back one thing someone tells you: 'So what you mean is... is that right?'

quiz.question: Why is reflecting back so useful in a conflict?
options: It delays the conversation
It lets you win the point
It shows you listened and catches misunderstandings early
It proves the other person is wrong
quiz.explanation: Feeling heard makes people more willing to listen, and checking avoids arguing about things nobody said.

cards.title: Look for the shared goal behind both of your positions
cards.body:
In a dispute, people usually state a position: 'I want to spend the holidays with my family.' 'I want us to stay home.' Positions clash. But behind each position is a need, such as wanting connection, rest, or to keep the peace with relatives.

Ask yourself and each other: what really matters to you here, and why? You will often find you want similar things, like a calm, happy holiday, but have different ideas of how to get there.

Naming that shared goal out loud changes the mood. It moves you from 'me against you' to 'us against the problem', and it opens up options that neither starting position allowed.
cards.apply_it: Think of a current disagreement and write down the need behind your position and the need you suspect is behind theirs.

quiz.question: What is usually hiding behind a fixed position in a dispute?
options: A desire to cause trouble
A deeper need or concern
Nothing; positions are all that matter
quiz.explanation: Positions often mask needs such as respect, security or rest, and these can be met in more than one way.

cards.title: Brainstorm options, then agree clear next steps
cards.body:
Once you both feel heard, list possible solutions together before judging any of them. Aim for several ideas, even silly ones, because one may spark a better one. Then talk through which options meet both of your needs best.

You probably won't agree on everything, and that's fine. Look for a fair compromise where both people gain something, rather than one person giving up completely.

Finally, make the agreement specific: who will do what, and by when. 'We'll try harder' fades fast. 'I'll text if I'm running more than fifteen minutes late, starting this week' is something you can both check. Agree to review it after a while and adjust if needed.
cards.apply_it: For one ongoing issue, list three possible solutions with the other person before choosing one.

quiz.question: Which agreement is most likely to work?
options: We'll both try to be better
Let's just forget about it
You need to change
I'll do the washing-up on weekdays and you'll do weekends, starting Monday
quiz.explanation: Specific, shared agreements with clear actions and timing are easy to follow and check.

cards.title: Apologise well: own your part without excuses
cards.body:
In most conflicts both people have done something they regret, even if it's only a harsh tone. Owning your part is one of the fastest ways to calm things down, because it invites the other person to do the same.

A good apology names what you did, shows you understand how it affected them, expresses genuine regret, and offers to put it right or do better. For example: 'I'm sorry I raised my voice. It made you feel small, and that wasn't fair. Next time I'll take a break instead.'

Avoid fake apologies like 'I'm sorry you feel that way' or 'Sorry, but...'. They shift the blame back and often restart the argument.
cards.apply_it: Think of one small thing you did in a recent clash and apologise for it clearly, with no 'but'.

quiz.question: Which is a real apology?
options: I'm sorry you feel that way
I'm sorry I snapped at you. It hurt you, and I'll take a break next time
Sorry, but you started it
quiz.explanation: It names the action, recognises its effect and commits to doing better, without shifting blame.

cards.title: Forgive to free yourself, even when you can't forget
cards.body:
Forgiveness is a choice to let go of resentment and the wish to get even. It does not mean pretending nothing happened, excusing harmful behaviour, or trusting someone again straight away.

Holding a grudge keeps the hurt alive in you long after the argument ends. Letting it go is mostly for your own peace. It can help to talk or write about how you felt, try to imagine what the other person was going through, and accept that forgiving often takes time rather than happening in one moment.

Remember to be fair to yourself too. Admit what you got wrong, learn from it, then stop replaying it. Small daily acts of forgiveness keep relationships healthy.
cards.apply_it: Write down one small grudge you are holding and one reason letting it go would help you.

quiz.question: What does forgiveness NOT require?
options: Letting go of the wish for revenge
Choosing your own peace over resentment
Forgetting what happened or excusing it
quiz.explanation: You can forgive while still remembering, setting boundaries, and rebuilding trust slowly.

cards.title: Know when to walk away or bring in a mediator
cards.body:
Not every conflict can be fixed by two people talking. If the same argument keeps going round in circles, it may help to bring in a neutral person, such as a trusted elder, a counsellor, a faith leader, an HR adviser or a trained mediator. They can keep things fair and help each side hear the other.

Some situations call for distance rather than discussion. If someone threatens you, hurts you, or constantly humiliates or controls you, your safety comes first. Step away, set firm boundaries, and reach out to people or local services that can help.

Walking away from a harmful situation is not failure. It is respecting yourself.
cards.apply_it: Name one neutral person you could ask for help if a conflict in your life gets stuck.

quiz.question: When is it wise to step away rather than keep talking?
options: When someone threatens, hurts or controls you
Whenever you feel slightly annoyed
Only after you have won the argument
Never; you should always talk it out alone
quiz.explanation: Safety comes first. Stuck disputes can use a mediator, and harmful ones call for distance and support.
